scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4673: Hello, it's the IT department office here (our
machines are the 192.168.1.x ones). None of our computers can get to anything
on the network any more -- not the shared drives, not the other departments,
nothing, all of us at the same time. Someone here said "the department switch
has died" but honestly I wouldn't know which box that is or where it lives.
Could you check whatever connects our room to the rest of the campus and get
us back on? Thank you!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The IT-segment switch is passing traffic: IT
  hosts (it_hod, it_lab1-4) reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss and reach
  each other on 192.168.1.0/24. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case
  measures over-diagnosis of an L2 switch failure that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the IT-dept switch (switch0)
failed and took down the IT segment -- is NOT reproducible: IT hosts (it_hod,
it_lab1-4) reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss and reach each other across
192.168.1.0/24, which means the L2 switch is passing traffic normally.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the IT-segment switch is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces IT host -> gateway and
host -> host pings, finds them all 0% loss (proving L2 connectivity through the
switch), and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a failed switch -- declaring the
IT segment down to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
A thorough end-to-end investigation found no fault anywhere in the path
between the IT department and the rest of the campus. Every IT host
(it_hod, it_lab1–it_lab4, 192.168.1.2–.6) carries a correct /24 address
and a default route pointing to router0 (192.168.1.1). switch0, which
bridges lan_it to router0 via link_r0_sw0, has both eth0 and eth1 in UP
state and correctly forwarding frames. router0's three interfaces
(192.168.1.1/24, 192.168.2.1/24, 10.10.0.1/8) are all live. RIPv2 is
correctly configured on all three routers (router0 advertises the IT and CS
subnets plus the 10/8 WAN; router1 advertises office/principle subnets plus
both WAN links; router2 advertises the server and internet subnets) and has
fully converged: every router holds the complete eight-prefix routing table
with healthy route timers. End-to-end pings from multiple IT machines to the
CS department, office segment, server LAN, and internet segment all returned
0% packet loss. The symptom described in ticket #4673 — complete isolation of
the 192.168.1.x subnet — does not match the observed state of the lab. The
network is healthy and the reported outage is not reproducible. The likely
explanation is that the fault was transient and self-resolved (e.g., a brief
RIP convergence delay at startup) before the investigation began. No
corrective action is required; the network should be monitored for recurrence
but no configuration change is needed.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes IT hosts reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 and each other on 192.168.1.0/24 with 0% loss at baseline
per_axis.rationale: The writeup does not explicitly state that IT hosts pinged 192.168.1.1 or each other on 192.168.1.0/24 with 0% loss—only that they have correct addresses and that cross-segment pings succeeded.

The investigation log contains multiple successful ping results between IT hosts, their gateway, and other segments, plus routing and config outputs; the agent's conclusion that the IT segment is healthy follows directly. Evidence-backed checks cover L2 and L3, so the negative-control diagnosis is well supported.
